questions.q: What is the author's central point?
options: Money can buy extra hours, so wealthy people should plan their days carefully
Budgeting articles in newspapers are the best guide to using one's time well
Time is unevenly shared, and geniuses should schedule their days like income
Time is the most precious equal daily supply, and we should manage it like an income
questions.explain: He says everyone gets twenty-four hours, and it should be managed with care.

questions.q: Why does the author call time an ideal democracy?
options: Everyone votes on how the day's hours are divided among citizens
Everyone gets the same amount; no wealth or genius earns more
Time can be traded freely, so the rich buy hours from the poor
Genius earns an extra hour a day, while wealth earns nothing more
questions.explain: No aristocracy of wealth or intellect; genius never gets an extra hour.

questions.q: What does the author say you cannot do with time?
options: Draw on the future or get into debt
Waste it as much as you please
Receive a fresh supply every morning
Spend it on work, rest or pleasure
questions.explain: 'You cannot draw on the future. Impossible to get into debt!'

questions.q: What title of essay has he never seen?
options: How to live on twenty-four hours a day
How to manage a household
How to live on eight shillings a week
How to save money
questions.explain: He's seen essays on living on money but never on twenty-four hours a day.

questions.q: What does the opening description of the man with a half-empty flat imply?
options: Luxuries are wasteful and should be given up by everyone
People fritter away resources, as many do with time
He needs a larger income to cover both needs and luxuries
He is secretly saving money to buy a better flat soon
questions.explain: He is used as an analogy for people who mismanage what they have, introducing the theme of managing time.
